clue.text: Lengthy pullover for an athlete

parts.note: lengthy means long
a jumper is the British word for a pullover sweater

explanation.surface: A long sweater suitable for a sportsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor in the field event of leaping as far as possible from a run-up is such an athlete.

clue.text: He's concerned with his image, being badly tailored

indicators.note: badly signals the letters of the following word are in a wrong order

explanation.surface: A vain man fretting about how he looks because his suit is poorly made.
explanation.walkthrough: The image is not a reflection but an idol, a worshipped figure.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol worshipper devotes himself to a graven image, so his concern is with images.

clue.text: Minister provides remedy without a word of thanks for showing up

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the remedy surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a cure is a remedy

indicators.note: in a down clue, showing up means the word is read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: ta is an informal British word for thanks

explanation.surface: A clergyman hands over a treatment but gets no thanks for turning up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for showing up' gives AT; 'without' is used in its old sense of outside. Minister is a church minister, not a government one.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant parish priest in the Church of England is a minister of religion.

clue.text: Life after death?

parts.note: suggests an afterlife, but means a life story written once someone has died

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds religious; it is a newspaper account of a life published after the death.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper notice of a death, recounting the person's career, is a short life story.

clue.text: Tight trousers Ian's ripped badly

indicators.note: badly shows that the letters of the words before it come out in a wrong order

explanation.surface: Ian's skin-tight trousers have split terribly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ripped' looks like part of the story but is fodder: IAN'S RIPPED is shuffled by 'badly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Very narrow-legged trousers, fashionable with 1950s Teddy boys, are named after narrow pipes.

clue.text: Jumper, pocket-size originally

parts.note: not a small sweater but a leaping animal that begins life tiny enough to live in its mother's pouch

explanation.walkthrough: After 1-down's pullover, 'Jumper' looks like clothing; here it is a leaping marsupial whose newborn grows in a pouch.
explanation.definitionFit: This Australian marsupial travels by hopping, and its young joey is reared in the mother's pouch.

clue.text: Exist with just a part interest

parts.note: to be is to exist
a half is just a part of the whole

explanation.surface: Being alive with only a share in something.
explanation.walkthrough: The word works in the phrase 'on behalf of', acting in someone's interest.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting on behalf of someone means acting in their interest or for their benefit.

clue.text: A boundary gives us the lead

definitions.meaning: the border or outer limit of something
an advantage over rivals, as in having the upper hand

explanation.definitionFit: Edge means both a border line and a slight advantage over a competitor.

clue.text: It's not even considered, mathematically

parts.note: 'not even' reads like 'not even thought about', but in arithmetic it describes a figure that cannot be split into two equal whole halves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even considered' suggests something ignored; the qualifier 'mathematically' switches to the sense of parity.
explanation.definitionFit: Integers that are not divisible by two, such as 3 or 7, are the opposite of even ones.

clue.text: In time chaps improve

indicators.note: the word 'In' at the head tells us the chaps are placed within the time

parts.note: AD (anno Domini) marks a time or era in dates
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Given time, the fellows will get better.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend something is to correct it and make it better, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Flirt and annoy worker

parts.note: to gall someone is to irritate or annoy them
the ant is the crossword's standard worker insect

explanation.surface: Someone flirts and irritates a fellow employee.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, a gallant is a dashing man attentive to women, a ladies' man or flirt.

clue.text: He doesn't appreciate the resort of Tangier

indicators.note: 'resort' read as re-sort, sorting the letters of the town's name again into a new order

explanation.surface: A visitor is unimpressed by the Moroccan holiday resort of Tangier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday destination but is read as re-sort, shuffling TANGIER.
explanation.definitionFit: An ungrateful person, one who shows no thanks for kindness received, is called this.

clue.text: Loose relative seen topless

indicators.note: without its top, so the first letter of the relative's word is removed

parts.note: an auntie is a relative

explanation.surface: A free-spirited family member is spotted sunbathing without a top.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a knot or a dog is to set it free, which is to undo or unfasten it.

clue.text: New proof is put to ninety-nine, half-asleep

indicators.note: making something new of the letters means arranging them afresh

parts.note: taken as written as part of the fodder
taken as written as part of the fodder
IC is 99 in Roman numerals (100 less 1)

explanation.surface: A fresh proof is checked at ninety-nine by a drowsy reader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' yields SOPORIF; 'put to' simply joins the Roman ninety-nine on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Soporific describes drowsiness or sleepiness, as when someone is barely awake and nodding off.

clue.text: Dispatches produce merriment on board

indicators.note: being on board a ship means being inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the ship is SS, steamship, which passengers come on board
laughter is merriment

explanation.surface: Reports bring amusement among those on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispatches' looks like news reports but means kills. 'On board' is the convention for putting something inside SS.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch an animal is to kill it, and to slaughter is likewise to kill.

clue.text: Last of the fighting in Europe for army unit

indicators.note: in places the end letter inside the word for Europe

parts.note: the Continent is the British name for mainland Europe

indicators.note: Last of means just the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: The final stage of combat in Europe calls for a body of troops.
explanation.walkthrough: To British speakers, 'the Continent' means mainland Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: A contingent is a body of troops supplied to a larger force, a military unit.

clue.text: He makes an example of one

definitions.text: He makes an example of one

parts.words: He makes an example of one
parts.note: reads as someone setting an example; in fact the word 'He' itself is a specimen of a certain grammatical class of words

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a man punishing someone as a warning; actually 'He' is a word, a grammatical example.
explanation.definitionFit: Words such as he, she, I and they stand for people, which grammarians class as this type of word.

clue.text: Bring the match alive when playing, before getting out

definitions.text: Bring the match alive when playing, before getting out

parts.words: Bring the match alive when playing, before getting out
parts.note: seems to describe a cricketer livening up a game; in cricket the batter facing the bowling is so described, and workers walking out are too

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batter who faces the next ball is said to be in this state, before being out; workers who walk out are too.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes both workers taking industrial action and the cricket batter about to receive the bowling.

clue.text: Brides eventually have tales to tell

definitions.text: Brides eventually have tales to tell

parts.words: Brides eventually have tales to tell
parts.note: brides in time become aged married women, and the phrase for popular superstitions joins them to tales

explanation.walkthrough: Old wives' tales are traditional beliefs passed on as folklore; brides eventually become old married women.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly married women are proverbially the source of folk superstitions, called their tales.

clue.text: Makes new plans about backing US soldiers caught in retreats

parts.note: RE means about or concerning, as in business letters

indicators.note: 'caught in' says the soldiers are held within the retreats

parts.note: dens are private retreats

indicators.note: backing means the soldiers' word runs backwards

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers

explanation.surface: Plans are revised over American troops trapped while withdrawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' gives SIG and 'caught in' holds it; 'retreats' looks like a verb of withdrawal but is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To redesign is to draw up fresh plans for something, so redesigns means makes new plans.

clue.text: Number of mischievous characters in digs

parts.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals
elves are mischievous little folk

explanation.surface: Several impish creatures are found in someone's lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' looks like British slang for lodgings, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To delve is to dig, so delves means digs, research deeply or burrow.

clue.text: More than one spoke of bones

definitions.meaning: the spokes of a wheel run from the centre to the rim, like lines from a circle's middle
the forearm bones on the thumb side, plural of the Latin anatomical name

explanation.definitionFit: Radii is the plural both of the geometric line from centre to edge and of the forearm bone.

clue.text: Outcome of rules being broken by team leader

indicators.note: rules being broken implies the letters are shattered and rebuilt in another order
leader means the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: What happens when the captain of the side flouts the regulations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being broken' yields RESUL; 'team leader' is the captain in the surface but simply a first letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A result is the consequence or outcome of some action or event.

clue.text: A responsible person

parts.note: reads as praise for someone reliable, but responsible here means the one to blame for a wrongdoing

explanation.walkthrough: 'responsible' suggests dependable; the sense needed is 'answerable for a misdeed'.
explanation.definitionFit: The guilty party, the one who committed the offence, is the person responsible for it.

clue.text: Young reporter has article on Caribbean island

parts.note: a cub is a young, inexperienced journalist
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A junior journalist files a piece about a West Indian island.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest island in the Caribbean Sea, ruled from Havana.

clue.text: Urging a dog to swallow a bone?

indicators.note: a dog swallowing a bone takes it inside, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a pug is a small breed of dog
the shin is the bone at the front of the lower leg

explanation.surface: Encouraging a pet dog to gulp down a bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushing someone to act is urging them on, pressing them forward.

clue.text: Some catch up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a trap is a device to catch something

explanation.surface: A little bit of catching up to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Part of something means some of it, not the whole.

clue.text: Novel house, but starting to let rain in

indicators.note: starting means just the first letter of the next word is used

parts.note: a roof that lets rain in has a leak

explanation.surface: A house in a novel whose roof is beginning to let the rain through.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's novel Bleak House supplies the definition: the answer is the word describing that fictional house.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens wrote the novel Bleak House, so this adjective names the house of the title.

clue.text: Sort of ruler and a clergyman for several parishes

indicators.note: to sort is to put in order, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A ruler of some kind, and a church official in charge of a district.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Church of England this cleric oversees a deanery, a group of country parishes.
